agent_notes: The superscription is numbered as verse 1 in the Hebrew (KJV 88:0), so every verse here is one ahead of the KJV. The terms מָחֲלַת לְעַנּוֹת and מַשְׂכִּיל are of uncertain meaning; I kept 'Mahalath' as a transliteration and offered 'sickness' / 'to afflict or to sing' as options in the commentary instead of choosing one. STEPBible glosses לַמְנַצֵּחַ 'to the choirmaster'; I kept it. Heman 'the Ezrahite' is not securely identified with the Levite Heman of Chronicles; the commentators split, and I say so.

STEPBible glosses לְעַנּוֹת as 'to sing' (root ענה, 'answer'); the other main reading is from ענה II, 'to be afflicted', which suits the psalm's tone. I glossed it neutrally as 'for afflicting / for singing' and flagged the ambiguity. Rashi and Ibn Ezra support the 'illness / affliction' reading; Metzudat Zion supports 'raising the voice'.

agent_notes: רְפָאִים is read as 'shades', the shadowy dead, against KJV 'the dead' (doubling מֵתִים). Rashi reads it as a wordplay on 'those who went slack' (רִפּוּ) from the root רפה; I give this as a noted etymology, not a claim of the text. Per the packet the root of רפאים and the root 'to heal' (רפא) are separate; the pun with 'heal' is my reading and no commentary in the packet states it.

אֲבַדּוֹן is rendered 'Abaddon' in the literal layer (the packet registry marks it as an entity); the dramatic layer uses 'the place of Destruction'. Metzudat David, Radak and Meiri all gloss it as the grave, and I follow them here instead of the later personification (Rev 9:11).

פִּלְאֶךָ is written as a plural-sense collective (STEPBible 'wonder[s]'); the five English versions all plural 'wonders'. I kept 'your wonder' in the literal layer to show the singular form and noted it.

agent_notes: Reviewer request addressed: the 'from youth' reading is now credited to Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David, who read מנער as 'since my youth'. Rashi is given as the alternative: sudden, choking death, with the word tied to 'shaking' (Exod 14:27). The English versions follow the 'youth' reading; Rashi's is the real alternative, since נֹעַר 'youth' and the root נער 'shake' are written identically.

אָפֻנָה is a hapax and its sense is uncertain. I gloss 'I am numbed/bewildered', close to KJV 'distracted', and give the Rashi and Radak/Meiri derivations in the note. The sources split between 'fixed' (Rashi, from אופן), 'fear' (Radak, Meiri, from פן 'lest') and 'turn away' (Metzudat Zion, Malbim). STEPBible has 'I am perplexed'.

KJV adds 'put ... into'; YLT 'is the place of darkness'. I keep it verbless in the literal layer. The dramatic layer follows the 'darkness is my only companion' reading, which also closes the psalm; this is my own reading.

agent_notes: חָפְשִׁי is a hapax-like sense here ('free', as in a freed slave), sitting oddly among the dead. KJV and Webster say 'Free among the dead'; ASV 'Cast off'; BBE reads it as 'my soul is among the dead'. I kept 'free' in the literal layer and explained the bitter irony in the commentary. The sources in the packet read it as release from duties and burdens (Ibn Ezra, Meiri, Metzudat David) or as a longing (Radak, Malbim).

KJV 'whom thou rememberest no more' renders a perfect (זְכַרְתָּם); the sense is the pluperfect or present, 'whom you do not remember'. I kept a plain past-present 'you do not remember them again'. Radak reads the past form as standing for a future; I do not follow him.

מִשְׁבָּרֶיךָ 'your breakers' is not 'waves' in the generic sense: the root is 'break', and the picture is of surf smashing. KJV 'waves' is acceptable but loses the breaking. סָמְכָה 'has lain / rests' is read as 'leans heavily' (the sense of 'support' turned to 'press'); Meiri lists several options, and I chose the one the five English versions mostly share.
